newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa stocks set to continue bull run next week.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa stocks set to continue bull run next week.

text.p: Fresh from a week of strong gains South African shares -- barring golds -- are expected to continue to rise next week as recent positive sentiment shows little sign of diminishing, dealers and economists said on Friday.
The bullish streak has been caused by a strong rand and soaring bond market, in marked contrast to most of 1996.
This has been coupled with expectations of a sharply improving trade balance this year which should cut the current account deficit and boost critically low foreign exchange reserves.
All in all, the picture looks remarkably rosy for short-term gains on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, commentators say.
"I am confident in this market at the moment. It has got off to a great start and this should continue in the short-term at least," said one portfolio manager who declined to be named.
However, one area of concern is the plummeting bullion price which on Friday fixed at its lowest level in almost four years in London.
The golds index is barely 100 points off its life-time low of 1,249.7 and little respite is seen in the short-term with some analysts predicting the gold price may drop into the low $330s an ounce.
"People are barely looking at the gold index these days. It is almost bombed out," said one dealer.

On Friday President Nelson Mandela gave an eagerly awaited speech at the opening of parliament in Cape Town. Mandela renewed a commitment to privatisation and the eventual scrapping of exchange controls, but said little to surprise the market.
Economists said the speech underpinned recent confidence in a country that has seen foreign institutions snapping up blue chip industrial stocks all week.

But some warned that the market should not get carried away with itself. Most see a steady rise up until Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's budget on March 12, when many are hoping concrete moves on exchange controls will be announced.
But any pieces of bad news could still upset the stocks bandwagon especially among foreign investors.
Dealers pointed out that a few foreign institutions had started to sell stock after news of violent riots in some Johannesburg suburbs linked to protests over water and electricity bill payments.
"A lot of this foreign money is short-term investment," said David Shapiro, head dealer at SocGen Frankel Pollack.
Dealers and analysts also pointed out that it was about this time last year that the rand began its dramatic fall on the international currency markets, scuppering a mood of bullish confidence.
"That completely turned everything on its head last year," Shapiro said.
